svg.aria-label: The dominant pattern in railway component inspection is locate then diagnose. Stage one runs a detector on a large image to find and crop every instance of a repeated part such as a fastener, dropper, insulator or bogie bolt. Stage two classifies the state of each crop, for example normal, missing, broken, loose or slack, often with a type-specific or multi-label classifier. A third, newer path skips labelled defects entirely: an anomaly model is trained only on normal crops and flags anything that does not look normal. The diagram contrasts the three paths and notes where each fails: the detector misses the part when it is missing entirely, the classifier needs examples of rare faults, and the anomaly model raises false alarms on texture changes such as rust or ballast.
svg.title: Locate, then diagnose: how railway component inspection is built
svg.text: Locate, then diagnose: how railway component inspection is built
Railway parts repeat thousands of times per km. Most pipelines find every instance first, then grade each crop.

g.text: Train on defect-free crops or strips (PatchCore, diffusion inpainting);
flag anything off-distribution. No defect labels needed.
Stage 1: a fully missing fastener leaves no object to detect — needs a "slot" model (expected position from sleeper spacing).
Stage 2: rare classes are tiny — hence GAN / style-transfer / 3D-model synthetic faults (one or two real samples is common).
Anomaly path: rust, wet ballast, grease and lighting look "abnormal" — false positives on complex rail texture remain the main complaint.
